items.title: Why is the pre-C++23 start_lifetime_as() function described in "Taking A byte out of C++" not exhibiting Undefined Behavior?
items.body:
In the talk "Taking a Byte Out of C++ - Avoiding Punning by Starting Lifetimes - Robert Leahy - CppCon 2022", the presenter shows the following code as a pre-C++23 alternative to std::start_lifetime_as:

template<typename T> 
[[nodiscard]]
T* start_lifetime_as(void* mem) noexcept{
    auto bytes = new (mem) unsigned char[sizeof(T)];
    auto ptr = reinterpret_cast<T*>(bytes); 
    (void)*ptr; 
    return ptr; 
}

The first line of this function is valid. It's starting a new lifetime of an array of bytes in the location of memory where mem is pointing at. Whatever was in mem (i.e. some type U) is no longer valid unless we use std::launder to access the memory there (as far as I understand, and this is explicitly said in the talk in a later example).

On the second line, we reinterpret_cast<T*>(bytes), which while I understand doing a reinterpret_cast is in itself not UB here, doing anything with that object would appear to be UB. The lifetime of object T has not started yet. Lifetimes of objects can't be started by reinterpret_cast, AFAIK.

On the third line, I have no clue why it is necessary. Even taking the previous lines at face value, the presenter towards the end starts talking about how they could have used std::launder instead, but because they didn't introduce std::launder yet and it would "be a pretty weird" use of std::launder, they decided not to use it here.

First, I don't understand how std::launder could be used. The object T still has not been created yet, and second why does de-referencing a void casting seem to "create" the object lifetime, as implied by the author?

I do understand type T must be an "implicit lifetime type" to work here, but I don't know how that changes the situation with respect to UB, if at all.

items.title: Is correctness of EBR algorithm guaranteed by `seq_cst` also guaranteed by changing them to RMW operations with `acq_rel` that write the same value?
items.body:
Consider this example:

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>

int main(){
  std::atomic<int> epoch = {0};
  std::atomic<int> value = {1};
  std::jthread t1([&](){
     epoch.store(1,std::memory_order::seq_cst);  // #1
     value.load(std::memory_order::seq_cst);  // #2
  });
  
  std::jthread t2([&](){
     value.exchange(2,std::memory_order::seq_cst); // #3
     epoch.load(std::memory_order::seq_cst); // #4
  });
}

In this example, if #2 read 1, then #4 must read #1, because it's guaranteed by the single total order #1 < #2 < #3 < #4. For other cases, #4 can either read the initial value or #1, they correspond to a valid single total order #3 < #4 < #1 < #2, or #3 < #1 < #2 < #4(or, #3 < #1 < #4 < #2), respectively.

If change the example to the following:

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>

int main(){
  std::atomic<int> epoch = {0};
  std::atomic<int> value = {1};
  std::jthread t1([&](){
     epoch.store(1,std::memory_order::relaxed);  // #1
     value.fetch_add(0,std::memory_order::acq_rel);  // #2
  });
  
  std::jthread t2([&](){
     value.exchange(2,std::memory_order::acq_rel); // #3
     epoch.load(std::memory_order::relaxed); // #4
  });
}

In this example, if #2 read 1, according to [atomics.order] p10

Atomic read-modify-write operations shall always read the last value (in the modification order) written before the write associated with the read-modify-write operation.

#3 must follow #2 in the modification order of value. Because their memory orders are acq_rel, #2 must happens-before #3, so the visibility of #1 to #4 is now guaranteed by the happens-before. Similarly, for other cases, #4 can either read 0 or #1. IIUC, these two programs are functionally equivalent in observable behaviors.

This first snippet of code is simplified from the EBR algorithm(i.e., Epoch-Based Reclamation). #3 emulates the operation that updates the pointer, the core idea is that, if #2 reads the old pointer value, it must precede #3 in the single total order, so #1 also precedes #4 in the single total order; therefore, #4 must see #1 to check whether the reader's epoch is the current one.

If we only consider the correctness of implementing the core idea(i.e., the EBR algorithm), can I change the memory order seq_cst to acq_rel by changing the corresponding operations to those in the second example? IIUC, they should have the same correctness; merely, the visibility of #1 is guaranteed by the single total order in the first way, and is guaranteed by happens-before in the second way.

Update:

A pseudo-implementation of EBR for multiple readers and a single writer is as follows:

#include <atomic>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

struct ThreadState {
    std::atomic<bool> active{false};
    std::atomic<uint64_t> local_epoch{0};
};

class EBRManager {
    std::atomic<uint64_t> global_epoch{0};
    ThreadState thread_states[8]; 
    
    // Bag[0], Bag[1], Bag[2]
    std::vector<void*> garbage_bags[3];

public:

    void reader_enter(int tid) {
        thread_states[tid].active.store(true, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
        uint64_t g = global_epoch.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst);
        thread_states[tid].local_epoch.store(g, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
    }

    void reader_exit(int tid) {
        thread_states[tid].active.store(false, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
    }

    
    void retire(void* old_ptr) {
        uint64_t g = global_epoch.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        garbage_bags[g].push_back(old_ptr);
        try_collect();
    }

    void try_collect() {
        uint64_t curr_g = global_epoch.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst);

        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
            if (thread_states[i].active.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst)) {
                if (thread_states[i].local_epoch.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst) != curr_g) {
                    return; 
                }
            }
        }


        uint64_t next_g = (curr_g + 1) % 3;
        

        uint64_t safe_g = (next_g + 1) % 3; 
        clear_bag(safe_g);

        global_epoch.store(next_g, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
    }

    void clear_bag(int index) {
        for (void* ptr : garbage_bags[index]) {
            free(ptr); 
        }
        garbage_bags[index].clear();
    }
};

struct Data {
    int value;
};

std::atomic<Data*> global_ptr{new Data{100}};
EBRManager ebr;

void writer_thread_update(int new_value) {
   Data* newData = new Data{new_value};
   Data* oldData = global_ptr.exchange(newData, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
   if (oldData != nullptr) {
      ebr.retire(oldData); 
   }
}

void reader_thread(int tid) {
   ebr.reader_enter(tid);
   Data* p = global_ptr.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst);
   ebr.reader_exit(tid);
}

My approach to proof:

As shown in the graph, we don't need to care about what the value of epoch at #1 reads; we can just assume that the value is C. Assuming the operation value.fetch_add(0,std::memory_order::acq_rel) at #2 reads the pointer value Px, we also don't need to care about what the writer does before, because the pointer value Px can only potentially be reclaimed after it is swapped out. So, we assume there exists a writer that executes an exchange operation that writes new_pointer and swaps out Px, because of the release sequence, this means, for any reader who reads the pointer value Px at #2 must synchronize with such a operation at #3 that swapped out Px and write new_pointer; therefore, its #1 must be visible to #4 of the writer. This is the core idea why I think fetch_add(0,acq_rel) can hold the same correctness as the first example does.

As shown in the picture, the epoch can at most be advanced once if the stored epoch of all readers reading Px equal G and the writer subsequently reclaims the pointer value saved in garbage[G-1]; anyway, Px was saved in garbage[G], the epoch cannot be advanced until all readers reading Px write false to active. This proof applies to any reader.

items.title: Is there any difference between the global module fragment and the `extern "C++"` blocks?
items.body:
When a module needs to include a header, the following usually doesn't work, since the header contents get attached to the module: (with function names getting mangled to include the module name, etc)

export module A;
#include <iostream> // Wrong

Including in the global module fragment does work, as it attaches the header contents to the global module:

module;
#include <iostream>
export module A;

Including in an extern "C++" block also seems to work:

export module A;
extern "C++"
{
    #include <iostream>
}

Some compilers warn about the latter, but that seems to be a generic warning for includes, that fails to check for extern "C++" above the include.

Is there any difference between the last two snippets? Other than the warnings, is there any reason to prefer one or the other?

(Note, I'm tagging c++20 because this is the version that introduced modules. If the answer is different for newer standards, I want the answer for the latest standard, not for C++20.)

items.title: typename in qualified member access
items.body:
I wonder whether this piece of code should compile and what function it should call. The situation is that there is a struct whose name matches that of a template parameter. My question is, inside the definition of the f<U> specialization (where U derives from T), does T mean the template parameter or the base class?

template<typename T> 
void f(T t) {
    t.T::~T(); // #1 should this compile?
    t.T::m(); // #2 should this compile? 
}

struct T { ~T() {} void m(){}}; // note named like the typename parameter
struct U : private T { ~U() {} void m(){}}; // note inherits from T

int main()
{
    f(U{});
}

Well, from naive look, it should compile #1 and #2, and find U::m(), and call the destructor of U;

But, I tried it on compilers using Godbolt https://godbolt.org/z/3KG8M5xvb and the behavior is not as I thought.

On Clang, it calls the destructor of U but it tries to call the base member function ::T::m() instead of ::U::m() leading to a compile error on #2.

On GCC, it calls the destructor of the base class U and the member function ::U::m() no compiler errors which matches my expectations.

MSVC raises errors on both lines saying it cannot access private base ::T destructor and private member function ::T::f().

Which compiler is correct, or is this implementation defined behavior?

I tried to read the standard to determine the answer but I don't understand it.

items.title: How to correctly determine the seed type for the various random number engines in the c++ standard library
items.body:
Recently there was a discussion on the reddit c++ subedit pertaining to the difficulties of using the random library. One of the issues was how to correctly seed a random number engines.

std::random_device r;
std::array<XXXXXXXXX,std::mt19937::state_size> seed;
std::generate_n(seed.data(),seed.size(),std::ref(r));
std::seed_seq seq(std::begin(seed),std::end(seed));

It seems based on how two of the major STL implementations do it, figuring out the input type of the seed sequence is not trivially knowable - not even attainable from the type traits by the looks of it.

MSVC: unsigned long 32 to 64 bits depending on the architecture libstdc++: always at least 32 bits but could potentially be larger depending on the definition of std::uint_least32_t

MSVC ( Microsoft Visual Studio Community 2022 Version 17.14.0 )

template <class _Seed_seq, _Enable_if_seed_seq_t<_Seed_seq, mersenne_twister_engine> = 0>
void seed(_Seed_seq& _Seq) { // reset sequence from seed sequence
    constexpr int _Kx = (_Wx + 31) / 32;
    unsigned long _Arr[_Kx * _Nx];  <=================|||||
    _Seq.generate(&_Arr[0], &_Arr[_Kx * _Nx]);

https://github.com/microsoft/STL/blob/main/stl/inc/random#L1489

GNU libstdc++

template<typename _UIntType,
    size_t __w, size_t __n, size_t __m, size_t __r,
    _UIntType __a, size_t __u, _UIntType __d, size_t __s,
    _UIntType __b, size_t __t, _UIntType __c, size_t __l,
    _UIntType __f>
  template<typename _Sseq>
    auto
    mersenne_twister_engine<_UIntType, __w, __n, __m, __r, __a, __u, __d,
             __s, __b, __t, __c, __l, __f>::
    seed(_Sseq& __q)
    -> _If_seed_seq<_Sseq>
    {
  const _UIntType __upper_mask = (~_UIntType()) << __r;
  const size_t __k = (__w + 31) / 32;
  uint_least32_t __arr[__n * __k];  <=================|||||
  __q.generate(__arr + 0, __arr + __n * __k);

https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/tree/master/libstdc++-v3/include/bits/random.tcc#L359

Question What should the type of XXXXXXXXX be and is there a way to determine this programmatically that is also portable between conforming compilers and standard library implementations?

items.title: Is this concept satisfaction a bug in GCC or did I invoke undefined behavior?
items.body:
Here's the test code:

#include <concepts>

template<typename T>
concept Printable = requires(T obj) {
    { obj.print() } -> std::same_as<void>;
};

template<Printable T>
void func(const T& obj)
{
    obj.print();
}

class Foo
{
private:
    void print() const { /* std::cout << "Foo" << std::endl; */ }

public:
    void bar() {
        static_assert(Printable<Foo>);
        func(*this);
    }
};

print() is a private member of Foo, so Foo shouldn't satisfy the concept Printable. But within bar(), print() is accessible, and it seems it mislead GCC to believe Foo satisfies Printable in the static_assert.
Additionally, it seems to fix/cache the value of Printable<Foo> to true, so in the line below, func(*this), GCC incorrectly tries to instanciate func<Foo> (believing Foo does satisfy Printable) then complains that print() is private.

MSVC, on the other hand, report an error at static_assert because of Foo not satisfying Printable

clang 20.1.0 (the latest on godbolt as I'm writing this question) has the same behavior as GCC, but the trunk build agrees with MSVC.

Godbolt link with the latest versions of compilers at the time of writing this question

Are GCC and non-trunk versions of clang in the wrong? Or perhaps did I invoke some undefined behavior?

items.title: Annotating intentional infinite loop to satisfy "-fanalyzer"
items.body:
I have a following embedded system optimization case (simplified).

int main() {
  while (1) { 
    // Do something
    if (unrecoverable_error) {  
      __breakpoint(); 
      while(1); 
    }
  } 
}

If the while (1); statement is replaced by return 0, the compiler invokes all the destructors due upon exit from main, (and for that matter generates the destructor code bloat) - both for main-local and global, even if the crt0 ultimately traps the CPU in a while(1); loop after all.

Thus, there is an advantage to judiciously use while(1); if one wants the system to intentionally hang.

Statically analyzing the code with -fanalyzer leads to (obvious) infinite loop error/warning.

How does one annotate that a specific instance of the infinite loop is indeed intentional?

I don't want to disable the infinite loop detection entirely (as it is possible that other parts of the code may contain bugs that lead to non-trivial infinite loops).

items.title: What constructors must be defined to satisfy copy constructible concept for any-like class?
items.body:
I would like to make a class that satisfies std::copy_constructible concept and in addition can be constructed from an arbitrary copy constructible value much like std::any does:

#include <concepts>

struct B {
    B(std::copy_constructible auto);
};
static_assert(std::copy_constructible<B>);

But unlike std::any the constructor template B(std::copy_constructible auto) receives its argument by value and not by reference. I expected that based on class.copy.ctor#5, such constructor is never instantiated for B type itself.

B must have implicitly defined copy and move constructors, which must satisfy the concept checking in the assertion. And indeed, GCC accepts the program just fine.

But MSVC dislikes it, gives a weird message about some uninitialized symbol:

<source>(8): error C2131: expression did not evaluate to a constant
<source>(8): note: failure was caused by a read of an uninitialized symbol

As well as Clang, which is more clear in its complains:

error: satisfaction of constraint 'constructible_from<_Tp, _Tp &>' depends on itself
note: while checking the satisfaction of concept 'copy_constructible<B>' requested here

Fortunately, both MSVC and Clang can be made happy by defining 4 user constructors:

struct B {
    B(const B&);
    B(B&&);
    B(B&);
    B(const B&&);
    B(std::copy_constructible auto);
};
static_assert(std::copy_constructible<B>);

Online demo: https://gcc.godbolt.org/z/rTh33cMG3

Which implementation is correct here?

P.S. There is a related question Class with constructor template requiring copyable argument is not copyable by itself, but it is about a simpler predicate std::is_copy_constructible_v and Clang's bug, which is fixed already in trunk.

items.title: Type hint a default return type used unless more specific overload exists
items.body:
Let's say I have the function

import numpy as np

def foo(a: float | np.ndarray, b: float | np.ndarray,
        c: float | np.ndarray, d: float | np.ndarray) -> float | np.ndarray:
    return a * b + c * d

It only returns a float when all input parameters are float. As soon as one of them is an array, an array is returned. How can I efficiently type hint that behavior? Using simple overloads I have to specify five variants.

from typing import overload

@overload
def foo(a: float, b: float, c: float, d: float) -> float: ...

@overload
def foo(a: np.ndarray, b: float | np.ndarray,
        c: float | np.ndarray, d: float | np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...

@overload
def foo(a: float | np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray,
        c: float | np.ndarray, d: float | np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...

@overload
def foo(a: float | np.ndarray, b: float | np.ndarray,
        c: np.ndarray, d: float | np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...

@overload
def foo(a: float | np.ndarray, b: float | np.ndarray,
        c: float | np.ndarray, d: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...

which, besides being a hassle, is not very transparent. and the problem only gets worse for more input parameters, of course.

Is there a way to tell the type checker that, unless the first overload is satisfied, the return type will always be an array?

items.title: Why does .NET 10 JIT not pass struct fields in registers despite physical promotion documentation?
items.body:
I'm trying to reproduce the "Improved code generation for struct arguments" optimization (physical promotion) described in the official .NET 10 Runtime what's new.

According to the article, for this code:

using System;
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;

struct Point
{
    public long X;
    public long Y;
    public Point(long x, long y) { X = x; Y = y; }
}

public class Program
{
    [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)]
    private static void Consume(Point p)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(p.X + p.Y);
    }

    private static void Main()
    {
        Point p = new Point(10, 20);
        Consume(p);
    }
}

the expected JIT output for Program:Main() should be:

mov edi, 10
mov esi, 20
tail.jmp [Program:Consume(Program+Point)]

My environment:

  • SDK: 10.0.301 (verified with dotnet --version)

  • Project: <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>

  • OS: Windows 11, x64

  • I created global.json to lock SDK version.

  • I run with: $env:DOTNET_JitDisasm="Main"; $env:DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0; dotnet run -c Release

However, here is the actual code that is generated:

; Assembly listing for method Program:Main() (FullOpts)
; Emitting BLENDED_CODE for generic X64 + VEX on Windows
; FullOpts code
; optimized code
; rsp based frame
; partially interruptible
; No PGO data
; 0 inlinees with PGO data; 1 single block inlinees; 0 inlinees without PGO data

G_M000_IG01:                ;; offset=0x0000
       sub      rsp, 56

G_M000_IG02:                ;; offset=0x0004
       mov      qword ptr [rsp+0x28], 10
       mov      qword ptr [rsp+0x30], 20
       lea      rcx, [rsp+0x28]
       call     [Program:Consume(Point)]
       nop

G_M000_IG03:                ;; offset=0x0022
       add      rsp, 56
       ret

; Total bytes of code 39

30

The struct is allocated on the stack and passed by reference (pointer in rcx), not in registers.

items.title: Why does `std::format_context` exist, if formatters implemented using it don't function correctly in some cases?
items.body:
The member function .format() of the std::formatter<...> specializations takes a parameter of type std::basic_format_context<OutputIt, CharT>, where CharT is typically char, and OutputIt is selected by the caller.

There is also a typedef called std::format_context that hardcodes OutputIt to an unspecified type.

Trying to use std::format_context in a custom formatter causes issues: the formatter mostly works, but e.g. trying to format a range of this type causes compilation errors:

run on godbolt.org

#include <format>
#include <print>
#include <vector>

struct A
{
    int x = 42;
};

template <>
struct std::formatter<A>
{
    constexpr std::format_parse_context::iterator parse(std::format_parse_context &parser)
    {
        return parser.begin();
    }

    // // ok:
    // template <typename T>
    // constexpr std::basic_format_context<T, char>::iterator format(const A &a, std::basic_format_context<T, char> &ctx) const
    
    // bad:
    constexpr std::format_context::iterator format(const A &a, std::format_context &ctx) const
    {
        return std::format_to(ctx.out(), "{}", a.x);
    }
};

int main()
{
    std::println("{}\n", A{}); // ok
    std::println("{}\n", std::vector{A{}, A{}, A{}}); // Error if using `std::format_context`.
}

The Formatter named requirement also doesn't seem to special-case std::format_context.

Why does the std::format_context typedef exist in the first place? It seems to be a honeypot for unsuspecting implementers of custom formatters.

basic_format_context is not constructible by the user, so I don't see where else format_context could be used if not as a parameter to std::formatter<...>::format().

My best guess is that it could be used if you absolutely can't template the formatting function for some reason, so this would allow you to hide the implementation, and have it work at least in the common cases.

items.title: NSight Systems fails to profile GPU activity: "No CUDA events collected. Does the process use CUDA?"
items.body:
I'm using CUDA 13.1. Whatever CUDA program I run, NSight Systems refuses to profile it, telling me that "No CUDA events collected. Does the process use CUDA?".

To give a concrete example, I can successfully build and run the vectorAdd program (from the CUDA samples repository; see below for a copy of it). With that done, I fire up nsys-ui, put in the program path and start profiling. The profiling concludes, and a timeline is visible, including CUDA API calls, but - there are several errors:

I also tried running the profiler as the root user; same behavior.

Why is this happening? Is there some modprobe setting I need to make? I don't think there's a problem with the CUDA installation itself, since when vectorAdd runs, it verifies the results have been computed correctly.

Edit: I get the same behavior with CUDA 13.0's bundled NSight Systems; but - with CUDA 12.9's NSight Systems - the profiling concludes sucessfully, no errors, and I see the memory transfers and kernel launches on the timeline. /**
 * Vector addition: C = A + B.

 * This sample is a very basic sample that implements element by element
 * vector addition. It is the same as the sample illustrating Chapter 2

 */

#include <stdio.h>

// For the CUDA runtime routines (prefixed with "cuda_")
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#include <helper_cuda.h>
/**
 * CUDA Kernel Device code
 *
 * Computes the vector addition of A and B into C. The 3 vectors have the same
 * number of elements numElements.
 */
__global__ void vectorAdd(const float *A, const float *B, float *C, int numElements)
{
    int i = blockDim.x * blockIdx.x + threadIdx.x;

    if (i < numElements) {
        C[i] = A[i] + B[i] + 0.0f;
    }
}

/**
 * Host main routine
 */
int main(void)
{
    // Error code to check return values for CUDA calls
    cudaError_t err = cudaSuccess;

    // Print the vector length to be used, and compute its size
    int    numElements = 50000;
    size_t size        = numElements * sizeof(float);
    printf("[Vector addition of %d elements]\n", numElements);

    // Allocate the host input vector A
    float *h_A = (float *)malloc(size);

    // Allocate the host input vector B
    float *h_B = (float *)malloc(size);

    // Allocate the host output vector C
    float *h_C = (float *)malloc(size);

    // Verify that allocations succeeded
    if (h_A == NULL || h_B == NULL || h_C == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate host vectors!\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Initialize the host input vectors
    for (int i = 0; i < numElements; ++i) {
        h_A[i] = rand() / (float)RAND_MAX;
        h_B[i] = rand() / (float)RAND_MAX;
    }

    // Allocate the device input vector A
    float *d_A = NULL;
    err        = cudaMalloc((void **)&d_A, size);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate device vector A (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Allocate the device input vector B
    float *d_B = NULL;
    err        = cudaMalloc((void **)&d_B, size);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate device vector B (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Allocate the device output vector C
    float *d_C = NULL;
    err        = cudaMalloc((void **)&d_C, size);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate device vector C (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Copy the host input vectors A and B in host memory to the device input
    // vectors in
    // device memory
    printf("Copy input data from the host memory to the CUDA device\n");
    err = cudaMemcpy(d_A, h_A, size, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to copy vector A from host to device (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    err = cudaMemcpy(d_B, h_B, size, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to copy vector B from host to device (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Launch the Vector Add CUDA Kernel
    int threadsPerBlock = 256;
    int blocksPerGrid   = (numElements + threadsPerBlock - 1) / threadsPerBlock;
    printf("CUDA kernel launch with %d blocks of %d threads\n", blocksPerGrid, threadsPerBlock);
    vectorAdd<<<blocksPerGrid, threadsPerBlock>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, numElements);
    err = cudaGetLastError();

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to launch vectorAdd kernel (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Copy the device result vector in device memory to the host result vector
    // in host memory.
    printf("Copy output data from the CUDA device to the host memory\n");
    err = cudaMemcpy(h_C, d_C, size, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to copy vector C from device to host (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Verify that the result vector is correct
    for (int i = 0; i < numElements; ++i) {
        if (fabs(h_A[i] + h_B[i] - h_C[i]) > 1e-5) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Result verification failed at element %d!\n", i);
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }
    }

    printf("Test PASSED\n");

    // Free device global memory
    err = cudaFree(d_A);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to free device vector A (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    err = cudaFree(d_B);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to free device vector B (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    err = cudaFree(d_C);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to free device vector C (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Free host memory
    free(h_A);
    free(h_B);
    free(h_C);

    printf("Done\n");
    return 0;
}

items.title: Convoluted operator<=> rules in case of mutually recursive std::variant
items.body:
Coming from C++17 and trying to integrate operator<=>. I've stumbled on a conundrum. There seems to be no way to implement a generic container-like class where its T is a mutually recursive std::variant. Everything is fine with a common set of pre-C++20 comparison operators, probably because they are completely defined at any point in time. Event if T is forward declared at the point of template declaration.

I've compiled a simplified set of test cases that make this issue evident. There Array and Map are not templated, but are simple structs, for simplicity, based on std::vector and std::map. This still clearly shows that comparison category type must be known upfront. Or operator<=> must be dropped altogether, with drawbacks (live on godbolt.com).

#include <compare>
#include <vector>
#include <map>
#include <variant>
#include <type_traits>

/// Set 1-8, to choose between cases
#define CASE 1
#define WANT_DEFAULT_WHEN_MEMEBER 0

/// Must be forward declared, as, e.g., using `std::vector<Var>` in Var's declaration would not be possible
struct Array;
struct Map;

using Var = std::variant<int, Array, Map>;


/// [CASE 1] Deduced comparison category type + default
/// [COMPILES] No compiler
#if CASE == 1

struct Array
{
    bool operator==(const Array & that) const = default;
    auto operator<=>(const Array & that) const = default;

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    bool operator==(const Map & that) const = default;
    auto operator<=>(const Map & that) const = default;

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

/// [CASE 2] Deduced comparison category type, declared outside, still default
/// [COMPILES] No compiler
#elif CASE == 2

struct Array
{
    bool operator==(const Array & that) const = default;
    auto operator<=>(const Array & that) const;

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    bool operator==(const Map & that) const = default;
    auto operator<=>(const Map & that) const;

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

auto Array::operator<=>(const Array & that) const = default;

auto Map::operator<=>(const Map & that) const = default;


/// [CASE 3] Declared outside, with concrete comparison category type
/// [COMPILES] Only in GCC 15.2
#elif CASE == 3

struct Array
{
    bool operator==(const Array & that) const = default;
    std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const Array & that) const;

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    bool operator==(const Map & that) const = default;
    std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const Map & that) const;

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

std::weak_ordering Array::operator<=>(const Array & that) const
{
    return value <=> that.value;
}

std::weak_ordering Map::operator<=>(const Map & that) const
{
    return value <=> that.value;
}

/// [CASE 4] Template hack to delay instantiation, deduced comparison category type
/// [COMPILES] Only MSVC 19
#elif CASE == 4

struct Array
{
    bool operator==(const Array & that) const;
    template <typename T, typename = std::enable_if_t<std::is_same_v<T, Array>>>
    auto operator<=>(const T & that) const;

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    bool operator==(const Map & that) const;
    template <typename T, typename = std::enable_if_t<std::is_same_v<T, Map>>>
    auto operator<=>(const T & that) const;

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

template <typename T, typename>
auto Array::operator<=>(const T & that) const
{
    return value <=> that.value;
}

template <typename T, typename>
auto Map::operator<=>(const T & that) const
{
    return value <=> that.value;
}

bool Array::operator==(const Array & that) const
{
    return value == that.value;
}

bool Map::operator==(const Map & that) const
{
    return value == that.value;
}

/// [CASE 5] Template hack to delay instantiation, concrete comparison category type
/// [COMPILES] All compilers
/// [LIMITATION] Requires knowing comparison category type, won't work if deducation is needed (template class)
#elif CASE == 5

struct Array
{
    bool operator==(const Array & that) const;
    template <typename T, typename = std::enable_if_t<std::is_same_v<T, Array>>>
    std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const T & that) const;

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    bool operator==(const Map & that) const;
    template <typename T, typename = std::enable_if_t<std::is_same_v<T, Map>>>
    std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const T & that) const;

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

template <typename T, typename>
std::weak_ordering Array::operator<=>(const T & that) const
{
    return value <=> that.value;
}

template <typename T, typename>
std::weak_ordering Map::operator<=>(const T & that) const
{
    return value <=> that.value;
}

bool Array::operator==(const Array & that) const
{
    return value == that.value;
}

bool Map::operator==(const Map & that) const
{
    return value == that.value;
}

/// [CASE 6] As friends, no template hacks, declared before the type is defined
/// [COMPILES] Only MSVC 19
/// [LIMITATION] Only as out of class friend (not critical)
#elif CASE == 6

struct Array
{
    friend bool operator==(const Array & _1, const Array & _2);
    friend auto operator<=>(const Array & _1, const Array & _2);

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    friend bool operator==(const Map & _1, const Map & _2);
    friend auto operator<=>(const Map & _1, const Map & _2);

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

bool operator==(const Array & _1, const Array & _2)
{
    return _1.value == _2.value;
}

auto operator<=>(const Array & _1, const Array & _2)
{
    return _1.value <=> _2.value;
}

bool operator==(const Map & _1, const Map & _2)
{
    return _1.value == _2.value;
}

auto operator<=>(const Map & _1, const Map & _2)
{
    return _1.value <=> _2.value;
}


/// [CASE 7] As friends, no template hacks, declared before the type is defined, concrete comparison category type
/// [COMPILES] Only MSVC 19
/// [LIMITATION] Only as out of class friend (not critical)
/// [LIMITATION] Requires knowing comparison category type, won't work if deducation is needed (template class)
#elif CASE == 7

struct Array
{
    friend bool operator==(const Array & _1, const Array & _2);
    friend std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const Array & _1, const Array & _2);

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    friend bool operator==(const Map & _1, const Map & _2);
    friend std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const Map & _1, const Map & _2);

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

bool operator==(const Array & _1, const Array & _2)
{
    return _1.value == _2.value;
}

std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const Array & _1, const Array & _2)
{
    return _1.value <=> _2.value;
}

bool operator==(const Map & _1, const Map & _2)
{
    return _1.value == _2.value;
}

std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const Map & _1, const Map & _2)
{
    return _1.value <=> _2.value;
}


/// [CASE 8] The full set of operators (pre C++20 way)
/// [COMPILES] All compilers
/// [LIMITATION] No `<=>` therefore, when contained by another class, that class can't default its `<=>`,
///              at least in clang, but others seem incorrect as there is no way to deduce comparison category type
///              I.e. won't work with `WANT_DEFAULT_WHEN_MEMEBER == 1`
#elif CASE == 8

struct Array
{
    /// Can't be defaulted: some type would be forward declared at that point.
    bool operator==(const Array & that) const;
    bool operator<(const Array & that) const;
    /// All other operators would follow here

    std::vector<Var> value;
};

struct Map
{
    /// Can't be defaulted: some type would be forward declared at that point.
    bool operator==(const Map & that) const;
    bool operator<(const Map & that) const;
    /// All other operators would follow here

    std::map<Var, Var> value;
};

bool Array::operator==(const Array & that) const
{
    return value == that.value;
}

bool Array::operator<(const Array & that) const
{
    return value < that.value;
}

bool Map::operator==(const Map & that) const
{
    return value == that.value;
}

bool Map::operator<(const Map & that) const
{
    return value < that.value;
}

#endif

/// Additional condition: defaulted `<=>` with a `Var` member
#if WANT_DEFAULT_WHEN_MEMEBER

struct Foo 
{
    auto operator<=>(const Foo &) const = default;

    Var v;
};

auto cmp = Foo{} <=> Foo{};

#endif


int main() 
{
    return Var{} == Var{} && Var{} < Var{};
}

As of yet I couldn't find a solution. Probably I'm missing something, hence this question was posted. None of the 'working' solutions are perfect. [CASE 8] is closest to perfection and is basically pre-C++20, but lacks operator<=> which blocks default declarations of this operator in any class it is a member of. The latter can be verified with #define WANT_DEFAULT_WHEN_MEMEBER 1.

It looks like defect to me. Or maybe I'm missing something and it is possible to define Array and Map without explicitly knowing comparison category type (std::weak_ordering in test cases)?

items.title: Two threads communicating across weak and strong memory models (non-cache-coherent PCIe), why a read barrier is needed?
items.body:
I have two threads communicating through a shared memory-mapped register (flag). Thread 1 runs on a weakly ordered CPU (RISC-V) in an embedded PCIe processor, and Thread 2 runs on the host, which is a x86-64 CPU. The goal is for thread_2() to return only after thread_1() has started (and vice-versa).

Here’s a simplified example:

// Thread 1: RISC-V
void thread_1(volatile int* flag)
{
    *flag = 1;
    while(*flag != 2) {
        membar_read(); // (1)
    }
}

// Thread 2: x86
void thread_2(volatile int* flag)
{
    while(*flag != 1) {}
    *flag = 2;
}

flag is initialized to zero before both threads start. membar_read() is an intrinsic.

Questions

  1. Without the barrier (1), thread 1 spins forever whil thread 2 finishes fine. How is this possible? items.title: std::ranges::minmax slower than std::ranges::min and std::ranges::max
items.body:
I benchmarked both solutions for finding the smallest and largest values within a range.

I would have expected std::ranges::minmax to be faster than using std::ranges::min then std::ranges::max as a single traversal should be made instead of two (as discussed there: Why need std::minmax_element?).

But to my surprise, if I didn't made a mistake, std::ranges::minmax seems slower (at least on https://quick-bench.com/).

What could explain this behavior? Is this a "bug" that should be fixed in the future?

Here is my bench: https://quick-bench.com/q/ohUNvsA5Egwl0oxgUFzChlD-2C8

And my snippets:

void use_minmax(std::vector<double> const& vec) {
    auto const [min, max] = std::ranges::minmax(vec);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(min);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(max);
}

void use_min_and_max(std::vector<double> const& vec) {
    auto const min = std::ranges::min(vec);
    auto const max = std::ranges::max(vec);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(min);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(max);
}

According to the documentation, std::ranges::minmax complexity is in the order of 1.5 times the size of the range (at worst) while using std::ranges::min and std::ranges::min is always in the order of 2 the size of the range. It implies that the actual number of operations for std::ranges::minmax is at worse: cx1.5xN where c would be surprisingly large.

NB: the naive implementation for single pass is actually faster (though not twice faster): https://quick-bench.com/q/lOJq7Eu913Qx1evPz4ICCiC_OaA

NB: I also benchmark on a local machine with -march=native and, though it changes the ranking, it does not change the global conclusion: single function version is slower than the 2 functions version.

[EDIT] here is a more exhaustive comparison, including the naive implementation: https://quick-bench.com/q/5_ibei8zFUM1y9RtM3k5EgnNtwU

With respect to all insightful comments about clang implementation, here is also the gcc benchmark: https://quick-bench.com/q/aAJ_AgZbAMmW5q5z3XEcchEQ69Q

It does not make a better work, though it is more consistent with respect with the two traversal versions.

In vertu of the Zero-overhead principle, this bench is bothering me.

[EDIT2] thanks to Peter Cordes comments, here are benchmark with int:

  • gcc: https://quick-bench.com/q/kyL4woieCXme5AvS_qCOCxWmjZM
  • clang: https://quick-bench.com/q/bptxi21holDI0q5INiSsrsKVN5g

(I made them more generic with respect to handled type in order to allow for more experimentations)

items.body:
I created simple string class with construct from only constant strings (literal or const char[])

template<typename T>
struct const_lit;

template<unsigned N>

When I use it as function param, it work well:

void check_func(str s) {}

...

But when I pass a function to a template function, no matter as a template parameter or as a function argument, then the GCC cannot use it inside function.

<ToggleButton PreviewMouseDown="ToggleButton_OnPreviewMouseDown"/>

private void ToggleButton_OnPreviewMouseDown(object sender, MouseButtonEventArgs e)

((ToggleButton)sender).IsChecked = !((ToggleButton)sender).IsChecked;

items.body:
I wrote a small program for a university assignment and got a surprising result: the Debug configuration runs faster than Release, and the code compiled for x86_64 (emulated) runs faster than the native arm64 build.

System

  • MacBook M4

  • 12 cores

  • 24 GB RAM

I built the project in CLion and tried different compilers — the result is the same.

CMake options used

DebugX86:  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=x86_64 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
ReleaseX86: -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=x86_64 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
DebugARM:  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
ReleaseARM: -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

Source code

// Parameters
long long counter;
int val = 1;
#define NUMBER 10000000001ll

void fun1(int a, long long start, long long stop, long long *pcounter) {
    volatile long long count = 0; // volatile so it is not completely optimized away
    for (long long i = start; i < stop; ++i) {
        if (i & 1) count -= a;
        else count += a;
    }
    *pcounter = count;
}

double test1(void) {
    auto t0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    long long cnt1 = 0;
    fun1(val, 0, NUMBER, &cnt1);
    counter = cnt1;
    auto t1 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    double ms = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>>(t1 - t0).count();
    return ms;
}

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    std::cout << "NUMBER = " << NUMBER << "\n";
    std::cout << "val = " << val << "\n";

    {
        std::cout << "Running test1 (single-threaded) ...\n";
        double ms = test1();
        std::cout << " test1: time = " << ms << " ms, counter = " << counter << "\n";
    }
}

items.title: Is creating an object not the same thing as starting its lifetime?
items.body:
I've always assumed that "creating an object" is the same thing as "starting its lifetime" (and not the same thing as allocating storage for it).

But I've recently been told that "creating an object" means something else, and that starting object's lifetime recursively creates all its subobjects, even it doesn't start their lifetimes, e.g.:

  • When starting the lifetime of a union without setting an active element, all the elements still get created.

  • When the lifetime of an array starts without starting the lifetime of elements, e.g. by std::allocator::allocate() or implicitly, all the element subobjects still get created.

I can't find a direct confirmation of this, but consider e.g. that:

  • The wording for & says it returns the address of an object, and applying it to an inactive element of a union is obviously legal.

  • The wording on std::allocator::allocate that says that it returns the pointer to the first element of the array, which I assume requires it to have been created (or there would be no object to point to).

Is this interpretation correct? Is "creating an object" different from "starting its lifetime"? If yes, do we have wording that more explicitly confirms this?

Note that this is a language-lawyer question. I'm interested in what the standard has to say about it, this wording quirk likely doesn't affect what happens in practice.

items.title: Finding a maximum "score" of a permutation
items.body:
Consider an array of a permutation P of length n (n > 2), namely some order of the integers 1 through n.

Example of P with length n = 7, [6,5,2,3,7,1,4]

A "score" of a permutation is measured by the amount of indices i (0 <= i <= n-3) that satisfy the condition, P[i] >= P[i+1] + P[i+2].

The score of the example P is 2 at i = 1, 5 (5 >= 2 + 3, 7 >= 1 + 4)

Could we find the maximum score among all possible permutation of length n?

Here are some bruteforce solutions:

n = 3; max = 1 (3 2 1)
n = 4; max = 2 (4 3 1 2)
n = 5; max = 2 (5 4 3 1 2)
n = 6; max = 2 (6 4 2 1 3 5)
n = 7; max = 3 (7 5 1 4 6 3 2)*
n = 8; max = 4 (8 5 3 2 7 6 1 4)
n = 9; max = 4 (9 8 5 3 2 7 6 1 4)
n = 10; max = 5 (10 8 2 6 9 5 4 1 3 7)
n = 11; max = 5 (11 10 8 2 6 9 5 4 1 3 7)
n = 12; max = 6 (12 7 3 4 10 9 1 6 11 8 2 5)
.
n = 15; max (currently) = 8; (15 13 1 11 9 2 7 14 10 4 6 12 8 3 5)
.
n = 20; max (currently) = 10 (20 15 1 10 19 14 2 9 18 13 3 8 17 12 4 7 16 11 5 6)

There seems to be a strategy of placeing digits in this manner:

20 15 1 10
19 14 2 9
18 13 3 8
17 12 4 7 
16 11 5 6

to achieve a 5 blocks of score = 2. But the solution of n = 15 with max = 8 suggests otherwise by joining 2 score 2 blocks

15 13 1 11
        11 9 2 7 | 14 10 4 6 | 12 8 3 5

Could we possibly find a formula or an optimal strategy for this? Thank you!

items.title: Is there a safe way to create directories with std::filesystem?
items.body:
I have compared the description of POSIX mkdir against

  • the description of std::filesystem::create_directory,
  • the specification draft for std::filesystem::create_directory, and
  • the specification draft for std::filesystem::create_directories

in face of what is described in 2612: Setting loose POSIX file permissions is security-sensitive of SonarQube:

In Unix file system permissions, the "others" category refers to all users except the owner of the file system resource and the members of the group assigned to this resource.

Granting permissions to this category can lead to unintended access to files or directories that could allow attackers to obtain sensitive information, disrupt services or elevate privileges.

effectively flagging uses of S_IRWXO on mkdir (and other similar functions).

Now, it seems to me that there is no way in which implementation based on C++ <filesystem> could be safe with regards to this problem.

If I read it correctly, I have two options to use <filesystem>:

  1. either I make a call using the simpler form (without coping attributes) and then follow with std::filesystem::permissions or
  2. I have a directory with correct attributes and I use it as copy base.

However, the first approach looks like a race condition. Between directory creation and permission settings an attacker could abuse the already existing directory. Furthermore, since <filesystem> API seems to be based on (text) paths, the actual directory could be somehow changed making the second call invalid.

While the second approach has uncomfortable requirements of the source directory and is still prone to the source directory changing the attributes before they are queried for base of the new directory.

Furthermore, it seems like the mkdirat functionality is not covered at all. Instead, since the API seems to be based on (text) paths, it is completely prone path components changing their "meaning" while functions are being executed.

Interestingly, as a side note, the cppreference.com and the specification draft seem to differ about behavior on Windows.

While from SonarQube description it seems like the <filesystem> case could be covered by ignoring create_directory issue and checking the subsequent permission call, I have not verified if that is the case. And also, it seems like the real problem would still be there under the hood.

Is there any way to make it safe with <filesystem>? I wonder why those create_directory / create_directories functions were designed this way...

items.title: Why does this C++ operator overloading code work in Clang but not GCC/MSVC with C++20?
items.body:
I recently encountered an interesting C++ code example that compiles with Clang (-std=c++20) but fails with GCC and MSVC. The code involves operator overloading and friend function declarations.

Code Example:

#include <iostream>

template<typename T>
class Foo;

template<typename T>
Foo<T> operator+(int, const Foo<T>&);

template<typename T>
class Foo
{
public:
    Foo(const T& val) : data(val) {}
    Foo operator+(int);

    friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);

private:
    T data;
};

template<typename T>
Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int num)
{
    return Foo(this->data + num);
}

template<typename T>
Foo<T> operator+(int num, const Foo<T>& other)
{
    return Foo(other.data + num);
}

int main()
{
    Foo<int> a(1);
    auto v1 = a + 2;
    auto v2 = 2 + a;
}

Compiler Behavior: Clang (17.0.1): Works with -std=c++20

GCC (13.2): Fails with error about operator+ not being declared

MSVC (v19.38): Similar failure

GCC has an error:

<source>: In instantiation of 'class Foo<int>':
<source>:35:15:   required from here
   35 |     Foo<int> a(1);
      |               ^
<source>:15:19: error: template-id 'operator+<>' for 'Foo<int> operator+(int, const Foo<int>&)' does not match any template declaration
   15 |     friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);
      |                   ^~~~~~~~~~~
<source>:22:8: note: candidate is: 'Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int) [with T = int]'
   22 | Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int num)
      |        ^~~~~~
<source>: In instantiation of 'Foo<T> operator+(int, const Foo<T>&) [with T = int]':
<source>:37:19:   required from here
   37 |     auto v2 = 2 + a;
      |                   ^
<source>:30:22: error: 'int Foo<int>::data' is private within this context
   30 |     return Foo(other.data + num);
      |                ~~~~~~^~~~
<source>:18:7: note: declared private here
   18 |     T data;
      |       ^~~~

Workaround: Swapping the order of operator declarations inside the class makes it work:

template<typename T>
class Foo
{
public:
    Foo(const T& val) : data(val) {}
    friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);
    Foo operator+(int);

private:
    T data;
};

items.title: How to safely handle thread join when interrupt signal (SIGINT) may arrive during join()?
items.body:
I’m facing a design issue in a multithreaded C++ program related to safely shutting down threads. Here’s the problem: My main program starts multiple threads. During shutdown, I call join() on each thread to wait for them to finish properly. However, while the program is stuck inside join(), an interrupt signal (e.g., SIGINT from Ctrl+C) can arrive. The signal handler immediately tries to stop all threads and also tries to join() again, or perform unsafe cleanup. This causes undefined behavior, because: There’s no way to know if a thread is already inside join(). join() is a blocking the call — if interrupted halfway, it’s unclear what the state of the thread object is. Double-joining a thread or touching the thread incorrectly can lead to crashes or deadlocks. I thought about sleeping for a short time instead of joining immediately, but that doesn't solve the fundamental race condition between: The main thread trying to join() The signal handler trying to "force stop"

My questions: How to properly design thread shutdown when an interrupt might arrive during join()? How to avoid unsafe behavior if a signal arrives during join()?

Important notes:

The signal handler currently calls _Exit(1) after trying to stop everything, which kills the program immediately (bad - this is how they implemented it for years, no clean shutdown).

I want to move toward a safer design any solutions?

items.title: Need clarification on how to capture by reference in C++ recursive lambda
items.body:
While writing a library that will be shared between programs compiled under GCC 14.2.0 for X86 and ARM 6.22 for Cortex-M, I came upon a discrepancy between how the two compilers handle the recursive lambda capture when using the new 'this auto &&' deduced 'this' feature.

Here is the code:

/* Compiled with --std=c++23 option */

struct Foo
{
  int s = 1 ;

  void zook (void)
    {
      auto f_ok = [ & s = s ] (this auto && f , int x) -> void // ok
        {
          if (x < 10) f (x + s) ;
        } ;

      auto f_bad = [ & ] (this auto && f , int x) -> void // error: invalid use of non-static data member 'Foo::s'
        {
          if (x < 10) f (x + s) ;
        } ;

      f_ok  (1) ;
      f_bad (1) ;
    }
} ;

The 'f_ok' lambda with the explicit reference capture of the 's' variable works fine.

The 'f_bad' lambda, which uses '&', should capture the 's' variable but generates a compiler error as shown in the code comments when compiled using GCC.

The ARM compiler accepts both versions and generates the same binary, but the GCC compiler complains for the 'f_bad' version.

I spend some time going deep into the woods of the C++ specification and was unable to determine what the standard says about this particular case.

I suspect at this point that there is a compiler bug in GCC.

In order to be certain, I need to know what the C++23 standard specifies regarding lambda captures under these conditions.

If anybody can shed some light on this, and/or perhaps point to the relevant part of the specification, I would appreciate it.

items.title: Primitive types in patterns: why doesn't Integer dominate byte?
items.body:
JEP 455 introduced Primitive Types in Patterns, instanceof, and switch as a preview feature in JDK 23. It continues as a preview feature in JDK 24 and 25, so the feature is not detailed in the Java Language Specification.

The JEP describes "safety of conversions", where certain pairs of types are unconditionally exact, meaning no runtime checks are required. For other pairs, a runtime test is necessary to determine if a conversion can be made without loss of information.

For example:

int x = getValue();  // Which returns 42

switch (x) {
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
}

The runtime check verifies that 42 will fit in a byte and matches, printing 'byte'.

If we change the order of the cases:

switch (x) {
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This will result in a compiler error because the int case now dominates the byte case.

Quoting from the Java Language Specification (where pattern dominance is defined),

A switch label in a switch block is said to be dominated if for every value that it applies to, it can be determined that one of the preceding switch labels would also apply.

So far, everything makes sense.

However, if we change the case for int to use the wrapper class Integer:

switch (x) {
  case Integer -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This code will compile without an error, and the result will be 'int'.

The compiler is clearly autoboxing the int to an Integer and matching the first case.

What I can't understand is why the compiler allows this, since the Integer case is still dominating the byte case. Any value that will match for a byte will also match for a boxed Integer.

JEP 507, the latest version states:

Furthermore, boxing conversions and widening reference conversions are unconditionally exact.

However, that still does not explain why the compiler is not rejecting this because of pattern dominance.

Just to be clear, all the examples use the same line, int x = getValue();, where getValue() returns 42.

items.title: Challenge spartaco
items.body:
SPARTACO/VPSI v1 — Open Cryptanalysis Challenge

A public challenge to the international cryptographic and cybersecurity research community

Author and developer: I. Villasmil
Research area: Applied cryptography, authenticated encryption, digital signatures, cryptographic key derivation, integrity verification, and formal security architectures.

1. Scientific Invitation

I formally invite cryptographers, mathematicians, cybersecurity specialists, academic researchers, and independent security laboratories to examine and attempt to defeat the cryptographic protections of SPARTACO/VPSI v1 using a publicly available collection of encrypted artifacts.

The challenge is direct:

Recover the original plaintext or protected cryptographic material from the released artifacts without possessing the legitimate secret material required by SPARTACO’s opening procedure.

All challenge files are my property, were generated for this experiment, and contain no sensitive third-party information. I expressly authorize independent cryptanalytic examination of these specific files.

The SPARTACO engine and its source code are not distributed as part of this challenge.

The published materials are the cryptographic artifacts themselves.

2. Technical Architecture

SPARTACO is a cryptographic protection and authorization architecture developed around the separation of integrity, identity, authentication, confidential recovery, and execution authority.

Its construction combines established cryptographic primitives with artifact-specific integrity commitments and a contractual authorization model.

The relevant mechanisms are:

AES-256-GCM — Authenticated Encryption

Document content is protected using AES-256-GCM, which combines ciphertext confidentiality with authentication of the encrypted data and associated authenticated information.

HKDF-SHA256 — Domain-Separated Key Derivation

The architecture derives cryptographic keys from account-associated input key material (IKM), using distinct derivation domains and artifact-binding context.

The four documented domains are:

  • K_AUTH — Authentication.

  • K_DEF — Authenticated defensive-state transitions.

  • K_DOC — Protected document opening.

  • K_REC — Content recovery.

These domains represent separate cryptographic authorities. Possession of material associated with one domain does not automatically grant the capabilities of another.

Ed25519 — Digital Signature Verification

The PRIV and KIT artifacts include externally signed canonical manifests.

Their Ed25519 signatures are independently verifiable using the supplied public key, rol_PUB.pub.

The signed manifests bind cryptographic commitments to the corresponding protected blobs.

SHA-256 — Structural Integrity

The protection scheme uses SHA-256 commitments for the artifact nucleus (nucleo) and its structural channels S and Q.

These commitments allow independent comparison of the protected bytes against their signed manifest representations.

SPARTACO Neutral Seal

The role packages additionally contain neutral-seal information associated with their protected content, including fragment-derived values and the #VPSI-NEUTRO:n marker.

SPARTACO-Ω — Contractual Mathematical Perimeter

SPARTACO’s broader authorization architecture includes mathematical invariants evaluated alongside authentication, integrity, resource binding, authorization, and lifecycle conditions.

The contractual acceptance rule is expressed as:

[

\mathrm{ACCESS_GRANTED}(r)

\bigwedge_{c\in\mathcal{C}(r)}c(r)
]

An operation is authorized only when every predicate required by its contract is satisfied.

The published challenge concerns the encrypted artifacts; the complete execution engine is not supplied.

3. Public Experimental Artifacts

The research corpus consists of four files:

FileFunctionrol_PRIV.pngPNG container holding sealed private signing material and an externally signed manifestrol_KIT.pngPNG container holding sealed keyset material and an externally signed manifestSC_IMG_9115.jpeg.spartacoStandalone AES-256-GCM encrypted document enveloperol_PUB.pubRaw Ed25519 public key for independent signature verification

The PNG role containers incorporate an spRt chunk containing their protected cryptographic package.

The standalone .spartaco document follows the document-encryption path and does not include the same outer Ed25519-signed manifest.

The supplied public key is sufficient for signature verification of the relevant signed packages. It does not provide the secret material used to derive the document-opening key.

4. The Cryptanalytic Problem

The challenge is to determine whether an independent researcher can recover the protected content from the released bytes.

The adversary is granted access to the complete published artifact corpus, including the raw public key and all exposed headers, signatures, commitments, ciphertext, and metadata.

The adversary is not supplied with:

  • The SPARTACO execution engine.

  • The legitimate account IKM.

  • The decrypted keyset.

  • The authenticated session material.

  • The document-opening key K_DOC.

Researchers may apply mathematical cryptanalysis, independent cryptographic implementations, structural analysis, and computational experimentation to the published files.

The investigation may address ciphertext confidentiality, key derivation, authenticated data binding, digital signatures, or possible interactions among the exposed cryptographic structures.

The central experimental question is:

Can the original protected plaintext be recovered using the published artifacts alone?

5. Evidence Required for a Successful Result

A successful confidentiality challenge result must demonstrate actual recovery of protected plaintext or protected cryptographic material from the released artifacts without the legitimate opening secrets.

A successful integrity challenge result must demonstrate an unauthorized modification or substitution that remains accepted under the relevant original verification conditions.

For scientific reproducibility, submissions should contain:

  1. Identification of the original artifact and its SHA-256 digest.

  2. A precise description of the cryptanalytic technique.

  3. Reproducible computational or mathematical evidence.

  4. The recovered plaintext or independently verifiable demonstration of the claimed result.

  5. A clear statement of the cryptographic boundary crossed.

Metadata extraction, successful public signature verification, or observation of ciphertext structure is not, by itself, a successful confidentiality break.

6. Experimental Authorization

I, I. Villasmil, creator of SPARTACO and owner of the challenge artifacts, expressly authorize researchers to download, copy, inspect, modify, analyze, and attempt to decrypt the published experimental files.

These artifacts were created specifically for public cryptographic research.

The authorization applies to the published experimental files, not to unrelated accounts, servers, systems, or infrastructure.

There is no requirement to obtain my private credentials or access my personal environment.

The purpose is to confront the cryptographic construction with independent mathematical and experimental investigation.

7. Public Research Repository

SPARTACO — Cryptographic Challenge

https://github.com/ilvervillasmil-ctrl/CHALLENGE-SPARTACO/tree/main/encryption_SPARTACO

This repository is an artifact-distribution repository, not a source-code release.

Researchers are invited to examine the published bytes, formulate cryptanalytic methods, reproduce their results, and submit technically documented findings.

SPARTACO/VPSI v1 — Independent Cryptanalysis Challenge

The encrypted artifacts are public. The cryptanalytic problem is defined. The invitation is open to the international research community.

I. Villasmil
Creator and Developer — SPARTACOSpartaco

items.title: Opaque type with static allocation in C; is this well defined?
items.body:
I want to hide the internals of a struct but also allow static allocation. Usually an API that provides an opaque pointer requires dynamic allocation (malloc and friends). However, for embedded systems, dynamic allocation is ideally avoided. I can expose another type with the same size and alignment to be used as a backing buffer - is this well-defined? Otherwise, is there a common solution or best practice for this sort of thing?

// foo.h
#include <stdalign.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#define FOO_SIZE 12
#define FOO_ALIGN 4

typedef struct foo *foo_handle_t;
typedef struct foo_static {
    alignas(FOO_ALIGN) uint8_t private[FOO_SIZE];
} foo_static_t;

foo_handle_t foo_create(void);
foo_handle_t foo_create_static(foo_static_t *static_foo);
void foo_do_something(foo_handle_t foo);
// Do not use if created using foo_create_static
void foo_delete(foo_handle_t foo);

// foo.c
#include "foo.h"
#include <assert.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

typedef struct foo {
    int x;
    float y;
    char *z;
} foo_t;

static_assert(sizeof(foo_t) == sizeof(foo_static_t));
static_assert(alignof(foo_t) == alignof(foo_static_t));

static foo_init(foo_handle_t foo)
{
    foo->x = 1;
    foo->y = 2.F;
    foo->z = "Hello";
}

foo_handle_t foo_create(void)
{
    foo_t *foo = malloc(sizeof(foo_t));
    foo_init(foo);
    return foo;
}

foo_handle_t foo_create_static(foo_static_t *static_foo)
{
    foo_t *foo = (foo_t *) static_foo;
    foo_init(foo);
    return foo;
}

void foo_do_something(foo_handle_t foo)
{
    foo->y += (float) foo->x;
}

void foo_delete(foo_handle_t foo)
{
    free(foo);
}

Reasons it might be UB:

  • Strict aliasing rule. Although, if the user never accesses the "private" member, then there is no aliasing.
  • Incompatible types. I believe foo_static_t and foo_t are considered incompatible types by the standard.

Thoughts

The biggest issue I can see with this is manually keeping the size and alignment synced with the static struct (which is different for each platform). I could just switch to C++ to get access specifiers. One thing I like about this, though, is that it doesn't expose any internals in the header (other than size and alignment). A C++ class header file will leak includes needed by its members (which can be avoided with the pimpl pattern, but then we're back to opaque pointers with dynamic allocation). Perhaps C++20 modules is the solution to all our problems...

Real-world Example

FreeRTOS queues solve this with their StaticQueue_t type, which duplicates the QueueDefinition type but renames all the members as dummy1, dummy2, etc. Surely I don't have to resort to this?

items.title: "Npgsql.PostgresException (0x80004005): 23505: duplicate key value violates unique constraint" while referencing ASP.NET Core Identity IdentityUser
items.body:
Project description

I'm following Clean Architecture's dependency rule in my app, so I cannot have IdentityUser in my Domain layer, to address this issue I followed Jason Taylor's approach from this Identity in Clean Architecture #399 discussion, however since I don't have a User entity I've defined only an ApplicationUserId property in my dependent entities.

public sealed class RefreshToken
{
    public Guid Id { get; set; }

    public Guid ApplicationUserId { get; set; }
}

My application user inherits from IdentityUser class in Infrastructure layer.

public class ApplicationUser : IdentityUser<Guid> { }

The relationship between application user and dependent entities is one-to-many. The configuration is defined in separate class.

public class RefreshTokenConfiguration : IEntityTypeConfiguration<RefreshToken>
{
    public void Configure(EntityTypeBuilder<RefreshToken> builder)
    {
        builder.ToTable("RefreshTokens");

        builder.HasKey(rt => rt.Id);

        builder.HasOne<ApplicationUser>()
            .WithMany() // no navigation property in ApplicationUser
            .HasForeignKey(rt => rt.ApplicationUserId)
            .OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict);
    }
}

The configuration is applied in ApplicationDbContext.

public class ApplicationDbContext : IdentityDbContext<ApplicationUser, ApplicationRole, Guid>, IApplicationDbContext
{
    public ApplicationDbContext(DbContextOptions<ApplicationDbContext> options) : base(options) { }

    public DbSet<RefreshToken> RefreshTokens => Set<RefreshToken>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder builder)
    {
        base.OnModelCreating(builder);

        builder.ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly(Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly());
    }
}

I'm using ApplicationDbContextInitialiser to recreate my database and seed it with the initial administrator account. Below are the methods I'm calling in this class, I've omitted the rest of the code for simplicity.

public async Task InitialiseAsync()
{
    await _context.Database.EnsureDeletedAsync();
    await _context.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync();
}

public async Task SeedAsync()
{
    var role = Roles.Administrator;

    if (!await _roleManager.RoleExistsAsync(role))
    {
        await _roleManager.CreateAsync(new ApplicationRole(role));
    }

    var email = "administrator@localhost";

    if (await _userManager.FindByEmailAsync(email) == null)
    {
        var administrator = new ApplicationUser
        {
            UserName = email,
            Email = email
        };

        await _userManager.CreateAsync(administrator, "Administrator1!");
        await _userManager.AddToRoleAsync(administrator, role);
    }
}

Problem

The problem is that EF Core generates a unique index on ApplicationUserId in the RefreshTokens table, even though the relationship is configured as one-to-many.

Because of this unique index constraint, the first request to the /login endpoint succeeds, and a refresh token is created and saved to the database, but subsequent requests to the same endpoint fail with the following error:

---> Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbUpdateException: An error occurred while saving the entity changes. See the inner exception for details.
 ---> Npgsql.PostgresException (0x80004005): 23505: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "IX_RefreshTokens_ApplicationUserId"

DETAIL: Key ("ApplicationUserId")=(the Guid of the existing application user) already exists.

    // stack trace omitted for readability

  Exception data:
    Severity: ERROR
    SqlState: 23505
    MessageText: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "IX_RefreshTokens_ApplicationUserId"
    Detail: Key ("ApplicationUserId")=(the Guid of the existing application user) already exists.
    SchemaName: public
    TableName: RefreshTokens
    ConstraintName: IX_RefreshTokens_ApplicationUserId
    File: nbtinsert.c
    Line: 666
    Routine: _bt_check_unique

What I've tried

I tried to fix this issue by explicitly configuring the index as non-unique, but EF Core seems to ignore this configuration.

// ...

builder.HasIndex(rt => rt.ApplicationUserId)
    .IsUnique(false);

// ...

Also, when I create a migration, EF Core still creates a unique index constraint.

// ...

migrationBuilder.CreateIndex(
        name: "IX_RefreshTokens_ApplicationUserId",
        table: "RefreshTokens",
        column: "ApplicationUserId",
        unique: true);

// ...

Why does EF Core generate a unique index on ApplicationUserId despite the explicit non-unique configuration and one-to-many relationship? How can I configure it to generate a non-unique index instead?

items.title: Get sum of calculated column in aggregated request
items.body:
Here is a simplified version of my table. It has two 'calculated' fields: calc1 and calc2 . And there is a method which calculates sums of specified fields:

import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, column_property
from sqlalchemy.ext.hybrid import hybrid_property

class TOne(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'TOne'

    RecordID: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)

    Amt1: Mapped[Decimal] = mapped_column()
    Amt2: Mapped[Decimal] = mapped_column()

    calc1 = column_property(Amt1 - Amt2)

    @hybrid_property
    def calc2(self):
        return self.Amt1 + self.Amt2

    @calc2.expression
    def calc2(cls):
        return cls.Amt1 + cls.Amt2

    @classmethod
    def get_aggregated(cls, session, *columns):

        columns_to_select = [
            sa.func.sum(c)
            for c in columns
        ]

        return session.execute(
            sa.select(*columns_to_select)
        ).one()

It works like this:

>>> print(TOne.get_aggregated(session, TOne.Amt1, TOne.calc1, TOne.calc2))
(Decimal('10'), Decimal('-15'), Decimal('35'))

The object this method returns is of type sqlalchemy.engine.row.Row and the problem is that names of the values of this tuple-looking object are sum_1 , sum_2 and sum_3 . I would prefer the names to correspond to the names of the columns; in this case the names I need are Amt1 , calc_1 and calc_2.

The SQL request this call produces is:

SELECT sum([TOne].[Amt1]) AS sum_1, sum([TOne].[Amt1] - [TOne].[Amt2]) AS sum_2, sum([TOne].[Amt1] + [TOne].[Amt2]) AS sum_3 FROM [TOne]

I want it to produce SQL request with different labels:

SELECT sum([TOne].[Amt1]) AS Amt1, sum([TOne].[Amt1] - [TOne].[Amt2]) AS calc_1, sum([TOne].[Amt1] + [TOne].[Amt2]) AS calc_2 FROM [TOne]

In order to achieve this I tried to specify labels like this:

class TOne(Base):
    .....
    @classmethod
    def get_aggregated(cls, session, *columns):

        columns_to_select = [
            sa.func.sum(c).label(c.name)    # <-
            for c in columns
        ]
    ....

It does work with 'usual' columns, but not with 'calculated' columns.
Looks like for calculated columns declared with colum_property I can use c.key instead of c.name but I am not sure if it is a reliable approach and would prefer a way which would work with all three types of columns.

items.title: Is JWTs considered a web resource?
items.body:
When building REST APIs requests should identify resources by using their URI, and Wikipedia says:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_resource#Using_HTTP_URIs_to_identify_abstract_resources

The concept of resource has evolved during the Web's history, from the early notion of static addressable documents or files, to a more generic and abstract definition, now encompassing every "thing" or entity that can be identified, named, addressed or handled, in any way whatsoever, in the web at large, or in any networked information system. The declarative aspects of a resource (identification and naming) and its functional aspects (addressing and technical handling) weren't clearly distinct in the early specifications of the web, and the very definition of the concept has been the subject of long and still open debate involving difficult, and often arcane, technical, social, linguistic and philosophical issues.

So when building authentication using JWTs in a REST API can the authenticate endpoint be something like /tokens/local or /tokens/github (for OAuth using github but using my server’s token). I don’t want to use /login or /log-in because they are verbs.

UPDATE: Based on Fielding’s dissertation: https://ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/rest_arch_style.htm#sec_5_2_1_1

The key abstraction of information in REST is a resource. Any information that can be named can be a resource: a document or image, a temporal service (e.g. "today's weather in Los Angeles"), a collection of other resources, a non-virtual object (e.g. a person), and so on. In other words, any concept that might be the target of an author's hypertext reference must fit within the definition of a resource. A resource is a conceptual mapping to a set of entities, not the entity that corresponds to the mapping at any particular point in time.

JWTs should be considered a temporal service right?

items.title: What's the difference between data member and member function references?
items.body:
Following How to define copy assignment operator to not be ill-formed across different CRTP children?, I have wondered what makes T& x() and T x() const (member functions) different from T &x (data members). Because when I used data members for tha aliases, it yielded this:

<source>:50:7: error: object of type 'Vector<float, 3>' cannot be assigned because its copy assignment operator is implicitly deleted
   50 |   foo = bar;                                   // foo should be { 4.0f, 5.0f, 6.0f }
      |       ^
<source>:41:6: note: copy assignment operator of 'Vector<float, 3>' is implicitly deleted because field 'x' is of reference type 'float &'
   41 |   T &x = this->values[0]; 
      |      ^
<source>:51:7: error: object of type 'Vector<float, 3>' cannot be assigned because its copy assignment operator is implicitly deleted
   51 |   bar = Vector<float, 3>{ size, size, size };  // bar should be { 1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f }
      |       ^
<source>:41:6: note: copy assignment operator of 'Vector<float, 3>' is implicitly deleted because field 'x' is of reference type 'float &'
   41 |   T &x = this->values[0]; 
      |      ^
<source>:25:14: error: non-const lvalue reference to type 'Vector<float, 3>' cannot bind to a value of unrelated type 'Details::VectorBase<float, 3, Vector<float, 3>>'
   25 |       return *this;
      |              ^~~~~
<source>:52:7: note: in instantiation of member function 'Details::VectorBase<float, 3, Vector<float, 3>>::operator+=' requested here
   52 |   foo += bar;                                  // foo should be { 5.0f, 6.0f, 7.0f }
      |       ^
3 errors generated.

However, using member functions, it works just fine and does not yield any mathematical errors whatsoever.

MRE:

#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>

/*
The problem applies to both the copy and move assignment operators.
*/

namespace Details {
  template<typename T, std::size_t N, class D> class VectorBase {
    public:
    T values[N];

    D &operator=(const D &rhs) {
      if (this != &rhs) {
        delete[] values;
        values = new T[N];
        copy(rhs.values, rhs.values + N, values);
      }
      return *this;
    }

    D &operator+=(const D &rhs) { 
      for (int valueIndex = 0; valueIndex < N; valueIndex++) {
        values[valueIndex] += rhs.values[valueIndex];
      }
      return static_cast<D&>(*this);
    }  

    friend D operator+(D lhs, const D &rhs) {
      lhs += rhs;
      return rhs;
    }
  };
}

template<typename T, std::size_t N>
class Vector : public Details::VectorBase<T, N, Vector<T, N>> {};

template <typename T>
class Vector<T, 3> : public Details::VectorBase<T, 3, Vector<T, 3>> {
  public:
  // T &x = this->values[0];

  T& x() { return this->values[0]; }
  T x() const { return this->values[0]; }
};

const float size = 1.0f;
Vector<float, 3> foo{ 1.0f, 2.0f, 3.0f };
Vector<float, 3> bar{ 4.0f, 5.0f, 6.0f };

int main()
{
  foo = bar;                                   // foo should be { 4.0f, 5.0f, 6.0f }
  bar = Vector<float, 3>{ size, size, size };  // bar should be { 1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f }
  foo += bar;                                  // foo should be { 5.0f, 6.0f, 7.0f }
  return 0;
}
